# 12-transload: sources

Back-test entry `12-transload.yaml`. Transload, YC Spring 2026 (Launch YC 2026-05-18; Launch HN 2026-06-09). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **HN**: Launch HN thread, founder post and replies. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48463273 (read whole through the HN Algolia API, https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48463273)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QP2-transload-we-measure-freight-with-security-cameras
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/transload
- **TTN**: Transport Topics, "Precision Pricing" (carriers' dimensioners in terminals). https://www.ttnews.com/articles/precision-pricing
- **FW**: FreightWaves, "Gov't lawsuit against YRC shines light on LTL reweighing practices". https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ltl-suit-against-yrc-spotlights-reweighing-practices
- **DTS**: Diversified Transportation Services, "How does a dimensioner work in a real-life environment". https://www.dtsone.com/dimensioner-actually-work-real-life-environment-2
- **SMC**: SMC³ blog, "Where LTL dock operations can improve shipper/carrier relations". https://smc3blog.com/where-ltl-dock-operations-can-improve-shipper-carrier-relations/

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the practitioner role, `dock_supervisor`; context actor).**
- HN: "transload helps LTL trucking companies measure freight dimensions using the security cameras already installed in their terminals." and "In practice, many terminals only measure a sample of their shipments."
- TTN (Estes): "A dockworker uses a forklift to drive the freight up to the landing zone".
- *My choice:* no public source names a job title (the shortlist scores this item 2 for that reason). I chose the **dock supervisor**, the person who runs a shift on the cross-dock and decides which freight goes to the dimensioner. That is where "only measure a sample" happens. A dock worker scans but does not decide what gets measured, and the revenue team only sees the result later.

**2. What (the job).**
- HN: "If a shipment is larger than the shipper reported, the carrier undercharges for it while still giving up the same amount of trailer space."
- HN: "carriers lose money every day because shippers understate dimensions and LTL is priced by volume."
- Job wording ("get every shipment billed at its true size without slowing the dock") is mine, combining these quotes with item 3's congestion point.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- HN: "The obvious fix is to measure every shipment, but thats impossible in a busy freight terminal. Dedicated dimensioning systems work for freight that passes through them, but they add forklift travel, create dock congestion, and change the normal flow of work."
- TTN: "We dimension a little more than 35% of our freight" (Estes). YRC about 40%, Oak Harbor about 8%.
- *My choice:* occasion "dock shift"; recall window 5 working days; Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5. The source says it happens on every busy shift but gives no count.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- HN reply: "Our wedge is underbilling in LTL trucking with ~10k relevant cross-docking warehouses across the US and Europe."
- YC-L: over 2 million irregular items move across the US by truck every day (as read on the page).
- *My choice:* market US. The company is based in Munich, but the US is the market its posts name first. Segment: dock supervisors at LTL carriers' cross-dock terminals in the US.

**5. Who pays (decision-maker role, buyer and payer, purchase friction).**
- HN: "We are currently working with several LTL carriers." YC-C: "transload helps logistics companies measure shipments using the security cameras they already have." YC-L asks: "Do you know any trucking company or warehouse owners?"
- *My choice:* the carrier pays. The **terminal manager** chooses (role id `manager`), and head office has to agree. Public material does not say who signs.
- Purchase friction, tested "An IT review of camera access": my choice. HN (kotaKat) gives a nearby signal: "you may need to look into NTEP approval before this is being used for legal trade... dimensioning is a big deal." Shared camera footage is the step most likely to need sign-off.

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- HN: "Our system has two main steps: connect a barcode scan to the right object in the video, then estimate that object's dimensions in real-world units."
- HN: "Dock workers already scan freight as part of the normal workflow. Each scan gives us a timestamp and a handling-unit ID."
- HN: "identify under-dimensioned shipments, attach visual evidence, and help carriers correct the billing or classification."
- HN: "Nearly every warehouse already has CCTV." Compatibility tests whether the cameras cover the doors where freight is scanned. That condition is my choice, because the mechanism needs it.
- Adoption friction, "Review each shipment the system flags": my choice. The output is a flag with evidence, and someone on the dock or in billing has to act on it.

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- HN reply: "We're seeing ~$50k/site/month in recoverable revenue from fixing that alone."
- YC-C: the founders put catching these differences at about $50k per site per month in rebillings and improved trailer utilization (as read on the page).
- *My choice, derived from the value claim:* no price is public. The founder's price belief is **$4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal**, about a tenth of the $50k claim, the share a value-priced B2B tool commonly takes. The cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$30,000 to $50,000 a month**. The top is the founders' $50k. The low end allows for the HN post's "roughly 10%" mis-measured against YC-C's "15%" (10/15 of $50k, rounded down). Ability to pay is derived by code: 8% to 20%, small share.
- `hourly_rate` $30: my choice, a round figure for an LTL dock supervisor's loaded hour. No source gives one.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- HN: "After spending time with customers and talking to more than 50 trucking companies, we realized that forklift routing was not the pain people kept bringing up. Freight dimensions were."
- HN: "For one customer, roughly 10% of checked shipments had dimension errors."
- HN: "Jago grew up close to this industry through his family's LTL trucking and cross-docking business."
- YC-C: "For our customers, 15% of shipments turn out to be bigger than what the sender claimed."

## The respondents

No public first-person account by an LTL dock supervisor or terminal manager was found. HN has no commenter who works on a dock, and searches of trucking forums and Reddit returned nothing on dimensioning. The shortlist warns not to invent customer voices. So **every story below is the author's invention, filling that gap**. Each is built on the trade-press facts named after it, and no real person's name is used.

Dock supervisors (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Marcus Bell: author's invention, filling a gap: no dock account public. Built on HN ("many terminals only measure a sample") and TTN (dimensioner lanes, Estes' 35%).
- Rosa Delgado: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on HN ("add forklift travel") and TTN (a disputed pallet a dimensioner photo showed was "72 inches tall").
- Dwayne Okafor: author's invention, filling a gap: the sceptic whose terminal already dimensions a large share. Built on TTN (Estes "a little more than 35%", YRC about 40%, "there are no long waiting lines").
- Teresa Lindqvist: author's invention, filling a gap: a small terminal with no dimensioner. Built on HN (sample only) and DTS ("Carriers base the size on the longest measurements in each direction").
- Hamid Rahimi: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Kenji Watanabe: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on FW: the dock staff "in charge of reweighing the freight" were separate from the "weigh and research department". So he picks the escape "Someone else does the checking".
- Lakisha Freeman: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). The sensitivity is grounded in FW's account of a federal lawsuit over reweighing practices.
- Brian Kowalczyk: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (no shift with unmeasured freight in the window).
- Priya Nair: author's invention, filling a gap: a terminal with a dimensioner on every inbound door, one down for an hour. Built on TTN (Estes "multiple units at our facilities").
- Samuel Mensah: author's invention, filling a gap: peak volume blocks the lane. Built on HN ("create dock congestion") and TTN (YRC: "we don't want a dockworker sitting and waiting on a dimension machine").
- Graciela Ortiz: author's invention, filling a gap: nothing measured, found at the trailer. Built on HN ("still giving up the same amount of trailer space") and SMC ("you're seeing more and more reclassifications on carriers' docks").
- Jerome Whitfield: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

Terminal managers (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only, no story by rule):
- Alan Brooks: author's invention, filling a gap: a manager whose own audit roughly matches HN's "~$50k/site/month".
- Fatima Benali: author's invention, filling a gap: counts the cost as inspection staff hours, not lost revenue (FW: a weigh and research department of "between 80 to 90 people" at one carrier).
- Ray Castellano: author's invention, filling a gap: cannot put a number on it, and head office decides.
- Nadine Fournier: author's invention, filling a gap: a smaller terminal with a smaller loss.
- Oluwaseun Adebayo: author's invention, filling a gap: a large hub where the loss is above the founders' figure.
- Greg Halvorsen: author's invention, filling a gap: the manager whose dimensioners already catch it and who sees no cost (TTN: Estes "using 129 dimensioners", "payback timeline is three to six months").
- Mei Lin Chou: author's invention, filling a gap: a mid-size loss and a long IT review.
- Dale Pruitt: author's invention, filling a gap: counts re-measuring hours, and someone else had to agree.

## Open

- **No job titles in the public material.** The dock supervisor and the terminal manager are my choices (item 1, item 5). A back-test may find the founders would have named the carrier's revenue or pricing team as the payer instead.
- **Price is derived, not stated.** $4,000 to $6,000 a month and the $30,000 to $50,000 cost are my derivations from the $50k value claim. Treat the commercial vector's reading as a reading of my derivation as much as of the founders' belief.
- **All twenty respondents are invented.** No dock or terminal manager voice was found in public. The stories are grounded in trade press (TTN, FW, DTS, SMC) and in the founders' HN post.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The founders' benefit is labelled "Every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample" under the nearest code, `easier_recovery` (revenue recovery). The label carries the meaning; the code name is approximate.
- **Decision-maker role id is `manager`.** The checker builds the Buyer and payer sentence from the role id ("The manager decides, and head office has to agree."), so the id was shortened from `terminal_manager`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional for a back-test. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM HOLDING_UP, SOLUTION PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Compatibility: camera access needs help or is missing at 3 of 7), COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice: most managers see far less than $30,000 to $50,000 a month).

whys.g1: The two answers name different obstacles -- Teresa has no cameras pointed at the scan doors, Dwayne says the paperwork is close enough and late trailers and short crews are what matter -- so a dock supervisor would leave them apart rather than in one group, and there are no groups to name badly.
whys.g2: There is no junk on this line, since both answers speak to what got in the way at the dock, so nothing junk ends up grouped.

founder.order_why: It runs from naming and market to context, problem, solution, then sending, which is how I'd explain Transload to someone: the dock and its unmeasured freight first, then cameras that measure it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 both carry the same question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.', so the context step seems to open twice around the recency screen (4).
founder.missing: Nothing asked who pays or what it costs. The terminal manager decides and head office has to agree, the price is $4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal, and the cost today is $30,000 to $50,000 a month. The flow also never asked about the sign-off step, an IT review of camera access, which is the friction I expect before any pilot.

PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked how many shipments I actually measure in a shift versus let through unmeasured, whether my lanes have dimensioners at all, how often I find misdeclared size after the fact, or how many flags per shift I could realistically review without slowing the dock. screens.why2: "Review each shipment the system flags" is how I'd say it to a dock supervisor, and the title and intro read clearly on first pass.
screens.why3: I know which effort worries me most: someone on the dock has to act on every flag during a busy shift, so I can answer this from my own customer conversations.
screens.why4: "Let the dock cameras be used to measure" is a permission that IT and the terminal manager give, not an effort a dock supervisor makes, so it overlaps with my purchase-friction item, and the option I'd want, scanning freight at doors the cameras cover, is missing.
screens.why5: My adoption effort is kept word for word, and the test sentence "Most would review each shipment the system flags" says what I believe.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? — Review each shipment the system flags / Scan freight only at doors the cameras can see

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, deciding whether to ask strangers for a pilot is the natural last setup step, and as a founder working with several LTL carriers I want leads from it.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot terminals is my own call and I know the answer at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two options are distinct, and there is no escape chip because none is needed.
screens.why5: The meaning is kept, but 'Leave your email' to a dock supervisor drifts a little, since a pilot here is a terminal and its cameras, which the terminal manager and head office decide on, not the supervisor alone.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you want to try this at your terminal? Leave your email and we'll talk to whoever decides." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs here, just before the link goes to dock supervisors, and nothing earlier in the flow asked it.
screens.why2: The hint mixes 'asks aloud on video' with 'records the voice you pick', so I had to reread it to work out whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both, and what the 400 credits pays for.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice a dock supervisor on a loud cross-dock shift would sit through, and the 5-second samples let me check.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with previews, a preselected default and the cost the same either way is a complete, distinct choice, and the hint covers people who would rather read and tap.
screens.why5: It keeps my respondents as 'dock supervisors' and leaks nothing about Transload's cameras or the terminal manager to whoever gets the link.
screens.instead: Who should ask dock supervisors your questions on video? (Daphne ▶ / Saskia ▶; the face and voice you pick are recorded once for this project, 400 credits either way, and every question is also written on screen to tap or type)

screens.why1: Choosing how dock supervisors will answer belongs right before sending, after who asks has been settled on the previous screen.
screens.why2: It reads mostly plainly, but the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' and 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' need a second read to understand that her video is still being made.
screens.why3: I know my supervisors answer between trailers on a loud dock with a scanner in hand, so the noise figure and tap-versus-talk choice are things I can judge directly.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap, or let them pick covers the real choices, and each comes with a clear readiness status.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'dock supervisors' wording and says nothing about Transload, cameras or terminal managers that would leak to respondents.
screens.instead: How should dock supervisors answer? — Daphne asks aloud on video (being recorded, ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap, and can speak or type into boxes (ready now) / Let them pick when they open the link

screens.why1: After choosing how dock supervisors answer, deciding who receives the links is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three options are plain and short, and 'Contacts page' and 'sign in with Google' are clear to a founder using the tool.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching carriers' dock supervisors through our customer and family LTL contacts by name or posting somewhere, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the real cases, but there is no option for a mix, such as named contacts plus an open link in a trucking group, which is how I would probably reach enough supervisors.
screens.why5: Nothing of the study is restated here, so nothing has drifted, and the screen only concerns delivery.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' is plain, but the number beside it, '3 holding · 7 people answered', reads at first like 3 of 7 people rather than 3 of 3 cards, and the deciding counts (4 of 5 at the bar on two cards) sit only on the cards, not by the verdict.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows its count and bar ('4 of 5 · bar 4 of 5'), but the page says 7 answered while every card counts 5, and nothing says why two people dropped out, so I need a second look to know who was counted.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the exact belief lines I checked, though the solution statement above them is garbled ('the dock supervisor software... flags... and gets back shipments flagged').
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what holding up means for Transload or what to do next, for example to check camera coverage at the doors before a pilot or to watch the two beliefs that only just reached the bar.
screens.why_b5: 'Holding up' rests on 5 of 7 with two cards exactly at the bar, and 'yes, with some steps' and 'on a condition' are counted for me without the thin margin or the small n being said.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: two of three beliefs sit exactly at the bar on 5 of 7 counted (2 not counted, because...), and camera coverage counts 'yes, with some steps' as yes, so confirm door coverage and IT access at a terminal before you price a pilot.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '4 of 5 said yes or yes, with some steps · bar 4 of 5 · at the bar', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts camera coverage at the doors as Yes 3, with some steps 1, No 1, over 5 people, and the strip's marker sits at 4, so all three read on first look; the count line explains that 6 answered and 5 were counted.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Compatibility and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: cameras already covered the doors where freight was scanned.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me camera coverage is not the blocker and points me to the adoption friction card, which is a concrete next place to look.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a lean, not a call', but the So line flatly says coverage 'is not what will stop them' even though the result sits exactly at the bar with 5 counted, so one more No would flip it.
screens.instead: Cameras covered the scanning doors for 4 of the 5 counted, exactly at your bar, so one more No would flip it; small terminals like Teresa's may have no camera on the doors, so check adoption friction next and plan for those sites.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 4 of 5 against a bar of 4 of 5, marked at the bar, so I know it held and by exactly what margin.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts whether it would have gone better over 5 people (4 a lot, 0 a little, 1 same), and the bar and marker sit at 4, so it is all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are word for word what I checked: every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates 4 of 5 and points me to Adoption friction, but it does not say what this means for my pitch, such as that the one no-difference came from a terminal already dimensioning heavily, or that one more such answer would flip it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Hamid's guess is excluded, it says plainly that this is a small group and a lean rather than a call, and it flags the answer as hypothetical, so nothing is overclaimed.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 5 against a bar of 4 of 5, with the one conditional yes called out, so I know it held and by what count.
screens.why_b2: Four Yes, one conditional Yes, zero against, five counted and the marker at 4 are plain on first look, though giving the bar both as 4 of 5 and as no more than 1 in 3 costs me a moment.
screens.why_b3: The title and the line 'Most would review each shipment the system flags' are what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and points 'below' to what would make it worth it for Dwayne, but nothing below says his condition, so I don't know what to change, such as making the evidence quick enough to clear a flag on a busy shift.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, Hamid's guess is left out and said so, the conditional yes is flagged, and 'a lean, not a call' keeps a five-person result from being called strong.
screens.instead: 4 of 5 would review every flag as is; Dwayne would if it was clearly worth it (his words: …). Make each flag's photo and dimensions enough to settle it in seconds, and check this again with more supervisors before counting on it.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' with '4 of 5 said yes or yes, with some steps · bar 4 of 5 · at the bar' right beside it, so I know it held and that it held exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b3: The name Compatibility and the line 'For most dock supervisors, cameras already covered the doors where freight was scanned' are word for word the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do: no line says that small terminals with only yard and gate cameras are the gap, or that I need a camera-install path or a minimum-site rule before I sell to them.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and 'at the bar' is honest, but nothing says five people is a thin base for 'held', and holding by exactly one person reads firmer than it is.
screens.why_b6: Teresa's quote teaches me something I did not type: small terminals have old cameras on the yard and gate and none on the scan doors. Dwayne's 'steps' quote is about paperwork and late trailers, not camera access, so it adds nothing to this line.
screens.instead: Held at the bar on 5: 4 had cameras on the scan doors. The 1 without was a small terminal with only yard and gate cameras, so check whether small terminals need cameras installed before you count them in the 10k sites. Relative advantage and Adoption friction need boxes here too.

screens.why1: As the opening gate it makes sense to ask first whether my dock had more freight than we could measure this week before asking anything else.
screens.why2: "Freight cross" with no "the dock" makes me read it twice, and "measured" leaves me unsure whether it means through the dimensioner or by any tape at all, since we hand-measure some and sample the rest.
screens.why3: I know exactly what went through my doors on my shifts this week and what went out the door without a dim on it.
screens.why4: Yes or No is right for a gate, but it shows two escapes when a gate should have none, and "I can't recall one particular shipment" doesn't answer a question about the whole week.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks through, but the founder's "crosses the dock" lost "the dock" and turned into a stiff restated line instead of a question about my week.
screens.why6: It is short and ends with "yes or no", but "did freight cross faster than it could be measured" sounds clipped heard once, because you wait for "cross what".
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did any freight leave your dock without being measured? Yes / No (no escape).

screens.why1: After asking whether freight beat the measuring this week, it makes sense to show me something that claims to measure all of it.
screens.why2: I follow most of it, but the opening 'Transload, flagged oversized shipments with video' reads broken, and on my dock we'd say it gets the dims or cubes the freight and checks it against the BOL, not 'fits a 3D box' or 'paperwork'.
screens.why3: Cameras on the doors, scans at the trailer, and freight billed under its real size are things I deal with every shift.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the name line has slipped out of shape, and the belief just repeats the barcode-to-video line instead of pointing back to it.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the first sentence sounds like a past-tense headline rather than saying what the product is, and the barcode-linking point comes round twice in a card that is already long.
screens.instead: Imagine Transload, software that measures freight from your terminal's cameras. As freight crosses, it ties each barcode scan to the freight on video, gets its dims, and flags anything bigger than the bill says, with the video as proof. The people building it believe it can do that with no change to how your dock works.

screens.why1: Asking whether my dock has cameras fits right after the video idea, but 'think of your last shipment' is an odd anchor when I push a few thousand bills across the floor a shift and the cameras belong to the doors, not to any one shipment.
screens.why2: 'Have cameras covering the doors' has lost its 'Do you' and reads like an order, so I'd read it twice; 'doors' and 'scanned' are my words, though.
screens.why3: I know which of my dock doors have cameras on them and where we scan freight, so I can answer this straight from my own floor.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but 'yes, with some steps' means nothing for cameras on doors; my real middle answer is 'some doors, not all'.
screens.why5: The card says 'oversized shipments', but my problem is freight not getting measured and billed at its true size, which isn't only oversized freight, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why6: It's short and the three options are easy to hold, but 'Have cameras covering the doors...' heard once sounds broken, and I'd have to work out that it's a question.
screens.instead: Think of your dock doors last shift. Do you have cameras on the doors where freight gets scanned? Yes, on all of them; on some of them; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After the idea card and the camera question, asking whether it would have helped is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I read it fine, but a shipment going better is vague to me, since freight either got measured and billed right or it did not.
screens.why3: I run a shift with hundreds of bills crossing, not one last shipment, so I would be guessing which one you mean and what better would look like.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and I can't tell fits as the way out.
screens.why5: The card line reads garbled, Transload flagged oversized shipments with video, so the idea comes through half said, and better for you drifts from billing freight at its true size.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options and one escape is easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: On your last shift, would Transload have caught more freight that was billed under its true size, or not? A lot more; a few more; no difference; fewer. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether Transload would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually put in the work it needs from me.
screens.why2: 'Review' is loose to me: it could mean watching the clip on a screen, or pulling the freight off the line to put it back through the dimensioner and reweigh it, and those are very different asks on a busy shift.
screens.why3: I'd be guessing, because whether I'd look at each flag depends on how many it throws per shift, and nothing here tells me if that's five or two hundred.
screens.why4: 'Yes' and 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' blur together, and the answer I'd most likely give is missing: I'd hand the flags to my inspector or the billing folks, not do them myself.
screens.why5: It keeps to the idea card's flagged shipments and doesn't push any terms on me beyond the product name I was already shown.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, four options I can hold in my head, and one escape at the end.
screens.instead: If Transload flagged a shipment as oversized, would you check the video and send it for a reinspection yourself, or not? — Yes, every one; Yes, if the flags were few; No, my inspector would; No, I'd ignore them; or say you can't tell.
